title: Probability
prerequisites: Familiarity with a deck of cards, dice and coins.
Comfort with fractions in lowest terms.

topics.title: Theoretical Probability
topics.quick_summary: Theoretical probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes.
topics.real_life: The probability of drawing an ace from a well-shuffled deck is 4/52 regardless of how many times you have tried before — the cards have no memory.

detailed.definition: For an experiment with equally likely outcomes, P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of possible outcomes). Two events are complementary if exactly one of them must occur.
detailed.key_idea: The phrase 'equally likely' is essential. A biased die or a bag with differently sized balls breaks the assumption, and the formula no longer applies.
detailed.working_principle: For two dice there are 36 equally likely outcomes, not 12 — the two dice are distinguishable even if identical in appearance. Listing the sample space as ordered pairs avoids this classic error.
applications: A deck has 52 cards: 26 red, 26 black, 4 suits of 13, 12 face cards.
Two coins give 4 outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT — not 3.
P(E) + P(not E) = 1, so the complement is often the quicker route.

points: P(E) = favourable outcomes / total outcomes, for equally likely outcomes.
Two dice give 36 outcomes; two coins give 4.
A deck of 52 cards has 4 aces, 12 face cards and 26 cards of each colour.
mistakes: Counting the outcomes of two dice as 12 or 21 instead of 36.
Assuming outcomes are equally likely when they are not.
Treating the ace as a face card; the face cards are jack, queen and king only.
topics.memory_hook: 'Favourable over Total' — and when the favourable cases are messy, count the complement instead.
topics.advanced: Equally likely outcomes are an assumption, not a fact, and a badly chosen sample space gives wrong answers. Bertrand's paradox shows that the same physical question can yield different probabilities depending on how outcomes are parameterised.

formulas.name: Theoretical Probability
formulas.variables: n(E) = number of favourable outcomes, n(S) = total number of equally likely outcomes.
formulas.when_to_use: For dice, coins, cards and any experiment with symmetric outcomes.
formulas.common_mistakes: Miscounting the sample space, especially for two dice or two coins.
formulas.shortcut: Use P(not E) = 1 − P(E) whenever 'at least one' appears in the question.
